title: 8 People Sealed In. The Oxygen Kept Vanishing.

scenes.text: It is September twenty sixth, nineteen ninety one. Sunrise over the Arizona desert, thirty five miles north of Tucson.

scenes.text: Eight people are about to be sealed inside this building, with four thousand other species, and no way to get food, water or air from the outside for two years.

scenes.text: Two hundred thousand cubic metres of sealed glass. Six thousand five hundred windows. The tightest seal anyone had ever built around a piece of the living world.

scenes.text: Five hundred people came to watch. The man closing the door is not a scientist. He is a Texas oil heir named Ed Bass, and this building is his money.

scenes.text: You're watching mindwired.
This is the story of Biosphere Two. What it cost, what it promised, what actually happened to the air inside it, and why the answer took two of the best geochemists alive to find.
scenes.videoQuery: Biosphere 2 exterior aerial glass domes Arizona

scenes.text: Not the engineers who built that seal. Not the chemists inside, testing the air every single day. And not the doctor, who would turn out to be the first person to notice something was wrong with him.
And why, thirty five years later, the thing everybody laughed at is still standing, still sealed, and still running experiments nobody else on Earth can run.

scenes.text: Chapter one. The ranch before the glass.
To understand how a building like this gets built, you have to go back to a ranch in New Mexico, twenty two years earlier.
scenes.query: New Mexico desert ranch adobe buildings

scenes.text: In nineteen sixty nine, a man named John Polk Allen founded an intentional community fifteen miles south of Santa Fe. He called it Synergia Ranch.

Allen was not a hippie drifter. He had a degree in metallurgical and mining engineering from the Colorado School of Mines, and an M B A from Harvard Business School. He also wrote poetry under the name Johnny Dolphin, and ran a theatre troupe called the Theater of All Possibilities.
scenes.query: John P. Allen Institute of Ecotechnics

scenes.text: In the early nineteen seventies the group founded something called the Institute of Ecotechnics. They built a research ship. They ran projects on four continents.
scenes.query: RV Heraclitus research vessel Institute of Ecotechnics

scenes.text: And somewhere in that decade, at that ranch, John Allen met Ed Bass, heir to a Fort Worth oil fortune, and one of the wealthiest men in Texas.
In nineteen eighty four they launched the project together. Bass paid. Allen invented. And a designer and architect named Margret Augustine ran the company that would build it.
Here is where the story splits, and where I have to be careful with you, because almost everyone in it is still alive.

In nineteen ninety one, a reporter for the Village Voice named Marc Cooper published a piece about the people behind Biosphere Two. He wrote that they were not, in his words, a group of high tech researchers on the cutting edge of science.
They were, he wrote, a clique of recycled theatre performers that had evolved out of an authoritarian, and decidedly non scientific, personality cult.
That sentence did more damage to Biosphere Two than any scientific result ever did. And it is an allegation, by a named journalist, in a named magazine. It is not a finding.
Because here is the part that almost never gets quoted alongside it.

The most credentialed early critic of the project was a botanist named Ghillean Prance, the director of the Royal Botanic Gardens at Kew. In nineteen eighty three he said their interest in science was not genuine, that they seemed guided by some sort of religious or philosophical system.
Prance then designed their rainforest.
And in nineteen ninety one, asked about it again, he said this. They are visionaries. And maybe to fulfil their vision they have become somewhat cultlike. But they are not a cult, per se.
scenes.source: Ghillean Prance, Phoenix New Times, June 1991
scenes.cap: “They are not a cult, per se.”

scenes.text: The man who first used the word took it back. Both are on the record, and if you only ever hear one of them, you are being sold a verdict.
In nineteen eighty seven, Discover magazine called Biosphere Two the most exciting scientific project undertaken in the United States since Kennedy launched us toward the Moon.
In nineteen ninety two, the journal Ecology called it New Age drivel masquerading as science.
Same building. Five years apart. Both of those are real quotes, and the truth is somewhere in the middle, and the only way to find it is to look at what the building actually did.
scenes.videoQuery: Biosphere 2 space frame glazing lattice interior looking up

scenes.chapter:
2 — THE NUMBER THAT
MADE IT SCIENCE
scenes.text: Chapter two. The number that made it science.

Three point one four acres under glass. Seven million two hundred thousand cubic feet of sealed air. Six thousand five hundred windows. And underneath all of it, a welded stainless steel liner weighing five hundred tons, so that nothing could seep up out of the ground.
scenes.videoQuery: Biosphere 2 glass pyramid ziggurat wide exterior desert

scenes.text: Inside, five wilderness biomes. A rainforest. An ocean, seven hundred thousand gallons of it, with a coral reef and a machine to make waves. Mangrove wetlands. A savannah. A fog desert.
scenes.query: The Ocean Biosphere 2 coral reef interior

scenes.text: Plus a farm, and a place for the humans to live.

Roughly four thousand species went in. Most of them collected by the crew themselves, on expeditions to jungles and reefs and deserts. Roy Walford, the crew doctor, later said the place became, in his words, our baby.
Now. Here is the number that decides whether any of this was science or theatre, and almost nobody tells you about it.
scenes.videoQuery: sunlight through greenhouse glass panes reflection

scenes.text: A greenhouse leaks. Every building leaks. The question is how much.
scenes.query: industrial silicone caulk seal glazing joint

scenes.text: The engineer responsible for the seal was William Dempster. He measured it two ways. He pumped the building to a slight overpressure and watched how fast it sagged. And he spiked the air with three gases that react with nothing, sulphur hexafluoride, helium and krypton, and watched how fast they thinned.
Both methods agreed. Biosphere Two leaked less than ten percent of its atmosphere per year.
That number means nothing to you yet. So here is Dempster's own way of saying it.
scenes.query: industrial silicone caulk seal glazing joint

scenes.text: There were about eighty kilometres of caulked glazing joints in that building. About sixteen kilometres of welded seam. Call it fifty miles of sealed glass and ten miles of weld.
And every flaw in all of it, every pinhole, every bad seal, every imperfect weld, added together, came to the equivalent of one single hole about nineteen millimetres across.
Three quarters of an inch. In a building the size of two and a half football fields.
scenes.videoQuery: Biosphere 2 exterior aerial glass domes Arizona

scenes.text: Hold onto that, because it is the reason there is a story at all.
scenes.videoQuery: condensation on glass greenhouse interior humid

scenes.text: There was a second engineering problem, and the solution to it is the strangest looking thing on the property.
Seal a building this tight and heat it with desert sun, and the air inside expands. It has nowhere to go. Nothing to push against but glass.
scenes.videoQuery: sunlight through greenhouse glass panes reflection

scenes.text: A wire service reporter put it plainly on the day they sealed it. Otherwise, he wrote, the heat and pressure would burst the glass walls.

So they built lungs. Two of them. Enormous domed chambers connected to the main structure by tunnels, each one containing a vast flexible diaphragm that rose and fell as the air inside expanded and contracted.
The building breathed. Not as a metaphor. Mechanically, every day, with the sun.
And it worked so well that the pressure difference between the inside and the outside of Biosphere Two stayed under eight pascals. About one thousandth of a pound per square inch.
There is one more detail from the construction that I think about a lot.
scenes.query: Desert Zone Biosphere 2 fog desert interior

scenes.text: They built a fog desert inside. It did not stay a desert. Water condensed on the underside of the steel and glass above it and dripped back down, and over time that section drifted toward chaparral, a wetter kind of scrubland.
scenes.query: Desert Zone Biosphere 2 fog desert interior

scenes.text: The building rained on its own desert. Nobody designed that. It is the first hint of the thing this whole story is about, which is that a sealed world does what it wants, not what you drew.
scenes.videoQuery: Biosphere 2 interior rainforest biome under glass

scenes.text: Chapter three. What they ate.
Eight people. Four women, four men, a split chosen deliberately after looking at how Antarctic bases and submarine crews hold together.
Roy Walford, sixty seven, the doctor. Abigail Alling, thirty one, marine biologist, first through the door. Mark Nelson, forty four, wastewater and wetlands. Linda Leigh, thirty nine, botanist.

Taber MacCallum, twenty seven, running the analytical chemistry lab. Jane Poynter, twenty nine, farm manager. Sally Silverstone, thirty six, co captain and tropical agriculture. Mark Van Thillo, thirty, technical systems.
Their job was to grow their own food inside two thousand square metres of farm. On paper it worked. Over the full two years they averaged about two thousand two hundred calories a day each.
On paper.
scenes.query: banana leaves lemon tree greenhouse interior

scenes.text: In the first six months the crops failed and the real number was one thousand seven hundred and eighty calories a day.
scenes.query: banana leaves lemon tree greenhouse interior

scenes.text: Broad mites got into the crops. Root knot nematodes got into the soil. And the two years they chose landed on back to back El Niño years, so the sky over Arizona was cloudier than the building had been designed for.
scenes.query: crop pests mites plant damage agriculture

scenes.text: Less light. Less food. Mark Nelson went in at a hundred and forty seven pounds and bottomed out at a hundred and seventeen. Taber MacCallum lost forty six pounds in six months.
Across the full two years the crew lost about seventeen percent of their body weight.

Nelson wrote about it afterwards. We experienced hunger throughout the two years, he wrote, and plates were always licked clean. And then this. I and many others ate our roasted peanuts whole, shell and all. We would eat anything to fill the stomach void.

On the day they came out, a reporter asked him about it. Nelson said the hardest thing was that hunger was a constant, nagging presence. He said it was hard even to watch a movie, because he kept focusing on what the actors were eating.
Jane Poynter said it took her four months to make a pizza. She had to grow the wheat, and thresh it, and feed and milk the goats for the cheese.
They ate so many sweet potatoes that their palms turned orange with beta carotene. Coffee was rationed to about one cup, per person, every few weeks.
scenes.query: banana leaves lemon tree greenhouse interior

scenes.text: And now the uncomfortable part, and I want to lay it out fairly because the man at the centre of it is dead and cannot answer.

Roy Walford was the crew's only physician. He was also, at that time, the most prominent researcher in the world on the idea that eating substantially less food extends human lifespan. He had founded the Calorie Restriction Society. He had been on that diet himself for years.
scenes.cap: The doctor was a caloric-restriction researcher.

scenes.text: The crew's daily food allotments were planned using Walford's own diet planning computer program. That is stated plainly in a paper written by two of the crew.
And when the farm failed and the calories fell, he published the crew as research subjects. Twice. In the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, and in a gerontology journal.
The mission's biggest failure became his dataset.
Walford knew exactly how that looked. He said so himself, unprompted.
I think if there had been any other nutritionist or physician, he said, they would have freaked out and said, we're starving. But I knew we were actually on a program of health enhancement.
scenes.cap: “I knew we were on a program of health enhancement.”

scenes.text: You can read that two ways and both are honest. The experiment's worst failure and the doctor's life's work pointed the same direction, and he was the only person inside qualified to make the call.
For what it is worth, his own follow up paper concluded that all eight of them came out in excellent health. That is also on the record.
Chapter four. The thing nobody invited.
While the humans were getting thinner, the sealed world was doing something worse.
Of twenty five small vertebrate species they put inside, nineteen went extinct.
And every single pollinating insect species died.

Think about what that means in a building where the humans have to grow their own food. The flowering plants inside Biosphere Two could no longer reproduce on their own. In a sealed world, that is a countdown.
What thrived instead was a species nobody had invited.

When they surveyed the site in nineteen ninety and ninety one, before closure, no ant species was dominant, and one particular ant, the longhorn crazy ant, was not present at all. Not one. It got in as a stowaway.
By nineteen ninety six, more than ninety nine point nine percent of every ant that came to a bait station inside Biosphere Two was that one species.

They did it by farming. The ants tended enormous populations of sap sucking insects on the plants and lived off the honeydew those insects produced. A closed loop, inside a closed world, that nobody planned.
Alongside them, cockroaches, which had been deliberately introduced to break down dead material, and which also ran away with the place.
The scientists who later wrote the most damning assessment of the whole project described what was left inside as crazy ants running everywhere, together with scattered cockroaches and katydids.

scenes.query: scientist analytical laboratory glassware testing air samples
scenes.text: Chapter five. The air starts going.
Taber MacCallum ran the analytical chemistry lab inside. Every day, he measured the air.
scenes.query: scientist analytical laboratory glassware testing air samples

scenes.text: Normal air is twenty point nine percent oxygen. That is what they sealed in with, on the twenty sixth of September, nineteen ninety one.
scenes.videoQuery: Biosphere 2 space frame glazing lattice interior looking up

scenes.text: Five months later it was eighteen percent.
scenes.query: scientist analytical laboratory glassware testing air samples

scenes.text: That is not a drift. That is a cliff. And it almost never gets told, because everyone jumps to the famous number at the end.
scenes.query: line graph declining chart scientific data

scenes.text: Then the fall slowed down. And kept going. Month after month, for over a year, roughly a hundred and forty parts per million of oxygen disappearing every single day.
scenes.query: line graph declining chart scientific data

scenes.text: Now remember the seal. Fifty miles of glass joint, ten miles of weld, one nineteen millimetre hole's worth of leak in the whole building.
scenes.videoQuery: sunlight through greenhouse glass panes reflection

scenes.text: The oxygen was not escaping. It could not escape. It was disappearing inside a sealed box, and the same measurement that proved it was disappearing also proved it had nowhere to go.
And there is a cruel piece of physics in here that I need you to understand, because it is why this got dangerous rather than just strange.
When you climb a mountain, the oxygen percentage stays the same. What drops is the pressure. Your body knows how to respond to that. Over weeks it makes more red blood cells. You acclimatise.
scenes.query: mountaineer high altitude thin air summit

scenes.text: Inside Biosphere Two the pressure never dropped. The lungs saw to that. Only the oxygen fraction fell.

So their bodies never got the signal. They were living at the equivalent of thirteen to fifteen thousand feet, and they could not adapt to it, because as far as their physiology was concerned they were still at three thousand eight hundred feet in Arizona.
scenes.query: mountaineer high altitude thin air summit

scenes.text: They started developing sleep apnoea. Waking in the night gasping, because their blood chemistry had changed.
So they ran oxygen lines from the analytical laboratory to the bedrooms, and slept breathing supplemented air, inside the sealed world that was supposed to make its own.

Jane Poynter described what those months were like. We were dragging ourselves around the Biosphere, she said. And everybody outside thought we were dying. The media was making it sound like we were dying. And I had to call up my mother every other day saying, no, Mum, it's fine. We're not dead.
And she gave it the name that stuck. It was like playing atomic hide and seek, she said. We had lost seven tons of oxygen. And we had no clue where it was.

scenes.chapter:
6 — THE SEAL WAS
NEVER A SEAL
scenes.text: Chapter six. The seal was never a seal.
While the oxygen was vanishing, the project's credibility was doing the same thing, and for entirely separate reasons.
About twelve days into the mission, Jane Poynter was feeding rice into a threshing machine on the farm and it took off the tip of the middle finger of her left hand.
scenes.query: crop pests mites plant damage agriculture

scenes.text: Walford reattached it inside. It failed. So on the eleventh of October, nineteen ninety one, sixteen days into a two year sealed mission, they opened the airlock and Jane Poynter walked out to a hospital.
She came back the same day. Out for a few hours. She lost the fingertip anyway.
On its own, that would have been a footnote. A medical emergency, handled, disclosed.
Except they did not disclose it. Not for almost three months. The public did not learn that the seal had been broken until the fourth of January, nineteen ninety two.

And when she came back through that airlock, she carried a duffel bag in with her. What was inside it has never been settled, and I am going to give you all three versions, because all three of those people are alive.
The company's own inventory said the bag held plastic bags, two reference books, maps showing where plants were, colour film, hydrochloric acid and spare computer parts.
Poynter's own account is that it held nothing of substance. Some circuit boards, she said, and a planting plan for the rain forest.

And then there is the allegation. A filmmaker named Louis Hawthorne, who had spent weeks on the site during preparation, told the Associated Press that his sources among the staff described two bags containing steel fittings, hydrochloric acid, and a handful of lead wire airlock tamper indicators.
The tamper indicators are the seals fitted to the outside of the doors. They are the physical proof that nobody has gone in or out.
scenes.query: lead wire security seal tamper indicator

scenes.text: The company's spokesman called that patently ridiculous. I have no way to settle it and neither does anyone else. All three accounts include the hydrochloric acid, and they differ on everything that matters.
But the bag is not what broke them. This is.
On the nineteenth of December, nineteen ninety one, the project acknowledged that it had installed a carbon dioxide scrubber inside Biosphere Two, and had not told anybody.
A machine that pulled carbon dioxide out of the air by blowing it through a falling curtain of sodium hydroxide solution. In a world that was supposed to be balancing its own atmosphere with plants.
On the same day, they also disclosed that six hundred thousand cubic feet of outside air had been pumped in to replace air that had leaked out.
That is the moment the press turned, and it never turned back. And the project does have an answer, in the peer reviewed record.

The scrubber was not a last minute panic. It was designed in from the start, in anticipation of the seasonal swing between photosynthesis in summer and respiration in winter. And crucially, it was designed to be reversible.
There was a furnace, whose job was to bake the captured carbon back out again in the summer and return it to the air, closing the loop.
Its heating elements failed. The loop was never closed. Across the entire two years, that furnace never once did the job it existed to do.
So which is it? A cover up, or a broken machine that a suspicious press found at the worst possible moment?
Here is the fact that settles what it meant, if not what it was. That scrubber removed about ninety eight kilomoles of carbon dioxide. Around four point three tons.
Set against the amount of oxygen that had gone missing, that accounted for almost nothing. Something like one and a half percent of the atmospheric carbon.
scenes.query: line graph declining chart scientific data

scenes.text: Whatever the scrubber was, it was not where the oxygen went. The mystery was still completely open. And the crew had thirteen months of it left to live through.
scenes.videoQuery: Biosphere 2 interior rainforest biome under glass

scenes.text: Chapter seven. The doctor couldn't add.
By January nineteen ninety three, sixteen months in, the oxygen inside Biosphere Two had fallen to about fourteen point two percent.
scenes.query: line graph declining chart scientific data

scenes.text: Roy Walford was the doctor. Sixty seven years old, the oldest person inside by more than twenty years. His job was to monitor everybody else's health.
He was also, it turned out, the most susceptible to the thin air of anyone in the building.
Jane Poynter tells what happened next, and it is the moment this whole story turns from a science experiment into something else.
And one day, she said, he couldn't add up a line of figures.
And it was time for us to put oxygen in.
The man measuring everyone else's decline was the instrument that finally registered it. He disqualified himself from duty. He could not do arithmetic.
scenes.query: handwritten column of figures numbers page

scenes.text: On a winter night in January nineteen ninety three, they broke the seal on purpose.
scenes.videoQuery: heavy steel airlock door closing industrial

scenes.text: Between day four hundred and seventy five and day four hundred and ninety four of the closure, pure oxygen was pumped into Biosphere Two from the outside world.
Nineteen days of it. Not a single dramatic moment, whatever you have read. A slow, deliberate, engineered rescue of a building's atmosphere.
Mark Nelson wrote about the moment they opened the door between their world and the fresh air on the other side.

We left a world with an oxygen level around fourteen percent, he wrote. Equivalent to being on a fifteen thousand foot mountain. In fact, we were at a three thousand nine hundred foot elevation in southern Arizona.
scenes.query: mountaineer high altitude thin air summit

scenes.text: Oxygen had been slowly disappearing for sixteen months. No one knew where it had gone. We were slowly climbing a mountain, but going nowhere.
scenes.query: mountaineer high altitude thin air summit

scenes.text: And then, when the air came in. In minutes, we felt decades younger. For the first time in many months, I heard the sound of running feet.
Chapter eight. In the walls.
So where did seven tons of oxygen go, inside a building that leaked the equivalent of one three quarter inch hole?
The obvious answer had been on the table from the beginning, and it had been ruled out. The reason it was ruled out is the most interesting thing in this story.
scenes.query: dark rich soil organic matter close up

scenes.text: Here is the obvious answer. Soil is alive. It is full of microbes, and microbes breathe. They take in oxygen and organic matter and they give off carbon dioxide, exactly the way you do.
scenes.query: dark rich soil organic matter close up

scenes.text: And the designers of Biosphere Two had deliberately packed their soils with organic matter, because they wanted the farm to be fertile. They wanted things to grow.
So the soil microbes had an enormous banquet, and they ate it, and they breathed while they did. Respiration outran photosynthesis. The building's soil was eating its air.
scenes.query: dark rich soil organic matter close up

scenes.text: Simple. Obvious. And provably wrong, because of one number.
scenes.query: line graph declining chart scientific data

scenes.text: Respiration is a one for one trade. Every molecule of oxygen that goes in comes back out as a molecule of carbon dioxide. If the soil had eaten seven tons of oxygen, the carbon dioxide inside that sealed building should have gone through the roof.
It didn't.
scenes.query: line graph declining chart scientific data

scenes.text: Dempster wrote it down plainly. The obvious explanation of loss to respiration was not evident, he wrote, because the implied increase of carbon dioxide did not occur. And furthermore, the atmospheric volume of Biosphere Two was shrinking.
So the mystery was never really that oxygen was vanishing. The mystery was that carbon dioxide was not appearing to match it. Two gases should have moved together. One of them didn't show up.
Which meant something inside that building was taking the carbon dioxide out of the air as fast as the soil was making it. Silently. Without a machine. Without anybody noticing.

They brought in outside help. Wallace Broecker, one of the most important geochemists of the twentieth century, the man who put the phrase global warming into the scientific literature. And a young researcher named Jeffrey Severinghaus.
And they did something clever. They went looking for the carbon by its fingerprint.

Carbon comes in different weights. Carbon twelve and carbon thirteen. And living things are slightly fussy. When a plant or a microbe processes carbon, it prefers the lighter one, which leaves a measurable signature behind.
So carbon that has been through something alive is isotopically different from carbon that hasn't. It is a tag. And it does not wash off.
They measured the isotopes in the atmosphere. In the biomass. In the scrubber's output. And then in the concrete.
Biosphere Two had fifteen thousand eight hundred square metres of exposed, unsealed concrete inside it. And concrete, when it is young, is not inert. It cures. It reacts.
scenes.query: concrete curing wall surface texture close

scenes.text: Calcium oxide in the concrete pulls carbon dioxide straight out of the air and locks it up as calcium carbonate. As limestone. Permanently.
scenes.query: concrete curing wall surface texture close

scenes.text: And when they measured the carbon locked inside that concrete, it carried the isotopic signature of something that had been alive.

The inner surfaces held roughly ten times the calcium carbonate of the outer ones. Somewhere between six hundred and seven hundred and fifty kilomoles of carbon dioxide. On the order of twenty five tons of it. Sitting in the walls.
scenes.query: concrete curing wall surface texture close

scenes.text: That is the answer. The soil microbes ate the oxygen, exactly as anyone would have guessed on day one. And then the building's own concrete quietly ate the evidence.
Two reactions in sequence, in a place nobody was looking. One famous, one so boring it happens on every construction site on Earth and nobody thinks about it once.
scenes.videoQuery: Biosphere 2 space frame glazing lattice interior looking up

scenes.text: Eight people nearly suffocated because their house was still drying.
scenes.query: concrete curing wall surface texture close

scenes.chapter:
9 — THE ONLY BUILDING
THAT COULD SEE IT
scenes.text: Chapter nine. The only building that could have seen it.
And now I can tell you why the seal mattered, and why I asked you to hold onto that nineteen millimetre hole.
scenes.videoQuery: sunlight through greenhouse glass panes reflection

scenes.text: The oxygen was falling by about a hundred and forty parts per million a day. That is a small signal. Dempster ran the simulations afterwards to find out how leaky a building would have to be before that signal disappeared into the noise.
scenes.query: line graph declining chart scientific data

scenes.text: The answer was a leak rate of one percent a day. Not a year. A day.
scenes.query: line graph declining chart scientific data

scenes.text: At that rate, fresh air seeps in fast enough to top the oxygen back up as it goes. An ordinary greenhouse would never have noticed.
Biosphere Two leaked less than ten percent in a year. It was, by a wide margin, tight enough to detect its own suffocation.
And here is the detail that finishes the argument, and it is a sad one.

After nineteen ninety six, when the project changed hands and the building was reconfigured for a different kind of research, they stopped maintaining that seal. The leak rate degraded to somewhere between one and two percent a day. About fifty times worse.
Which means the experiment that made Biosphere Two famous, the one thing it discovered that nobody else could have discovered, could never have been detected in the building it became.
It got exactly one chance to find that out, and the reason it found it is the thing everyone was laughing at. The obsessive, expensive, ridiculous tightness of the seal.
scenes.videoQuery: Biosphere 2 exterior aerial glass domes Arizona

scenes.text: Chapter ten. The door opens from outside.
They came out on the twenty sixth of September, nineteen ninety three. Two years and about twenty minutes.

Abigail Alling was first out. A reporter watching noted that she appeared to be trying to catch her breath as she stepped to the microphone. What she managed to say was, it's really a very different atmosphere.
They had also, by then, stopped speaking to each other. The eight had split into two groups of four.
I want to be careful, because the crew member who wrote the peer reviewed paper on that split deliberately declined to name who was on which side, and I am not going to do what he chose not to.
What is on the record is what the fight was about, and it is not what you would expect. It was not cabin fever. It was an argument that came from outside.

The project's owners were at war over the direction of the whole enterprise, and that war propagated inside. One group wanted to hold the closure absolutely. The other wanted to loosen it and import food.
Nelson compared it to the oldest argument on any Antarctic expedition. The sailors against the scientists.
Six months later, that war came for the building.

A second crew of seven was sealed in on the sixth of March, nineteen ninety four. On the first of April, federal marshals arrived with a restraining order and removed the entire on site management team. The new crew, told what was happening, initially thought it was an April Fool's joke.
scenes.query: federal court restraining order legal documents

scenes.text: Ed Bass put a banker in charge. A man who ran a Beverly Hills investment firm, and who would become considerably more famous two decades later, named Steve Bannon.
Three days after that, at three in the morning, two members of the original eight came back to the building they had lived inside for two years, and opened it.

Abigail Alling and Mark Van Thillo opened one double airlock and three emergency exits and left them open for about fifteen minutes. Roughly a tenth of the sealed atmosphere exchanged with the Arizona air. Five panes of glass were broken.
They had been suspended three days earlier. Alling's account, on the record, is this. I considered the Biosphere to be in an emergency state. In no way was it sabotage. It was my responsibility.
The company called it sabotage and was still calling it that two years later. Both of those are positions held by living people and I am not going to pick between them for you.
They were charged with burglary, trespassing and criminal damage, and released on twenty five thousand dollars bail each. And I have to be straight with you about something, because it matters.
scenes.query: federal court restraining order legal documents

scenes.text: I could not find out what happened to those charges. Two separate research passes, and the disposition of that criminal case is not in the public record I can reach. No verdict, no plea, no dismissal. So I am not going to imply one.
scenes.query: federal court restraining order legal documents

scenes.text: What I do know is that in June nineteen ninety six a jury in Florence, Arizona found in their favour in a separate civil case, over being fired. The Associated Press reported the award as nearly five hundred and twenty thousand dollars in lost wages.
The second mission was shut down early, on the sixth of September, nineteen ninety four. Nobody was ever sealed inside Biosphere Two again.
scenes.videoQuery: Biosphere 2 exterior aerial glass domes Arizona

scenes.text: Chapter eleven. The verdict.
In November nineteen ninety six, two ecologists, Joel Cohen of Rockefeller University and David Tilman of Minnesota, published the assessment in Science that has defined Biosphere Two ever since.
It is not gentle. Despite the resources, they wrote, it proved impossible to create a materially closed system that could support eight humans with adequate food, water and air for two years.
And the line that stings most. Almost unlimited energy and technology were available to support Biosphere Two from the outside.
Their conclusion is short enough to read to you in full, and it is, I think, one of the better paragraphs written about our situation on this planet.

At present there is no demonstrated alternative to maintaining the viability of Earth. No one yet knows how to engineer systems that provide humans with the life supporting services that natural ecosystems produce for free.
Despite its mysteries and hazards, Earth remains the only known home that can sustain life.
That is the prosecution, and it is fair, and it is quoted constantly. The paragraph immediately before it almost never is.

There may be a partial analogy, they wrote, between the initial problems of Biosphere Two and the early, well publicised flaws of the Hubble Space Telescope. Now that Hubble has been improved, it is a major instrument with the potential for observations never possible before.
Similarly, they wrote, research in a retooled Biosphere Two may well contribute exciting insights into the task of maintaining the viability of Biosphere One. The Earth.
The harshest critics Biosphere Two ever had left the door open. And then history walked through it.

scenes.text: Chapter twelve. What it became.
Columbia University ran it from nineteen ninety six to two thousand and three, and used that seven hundred thousand gallon ocean to demonstrate what rising carbon dioxide does to a coral reef.
scenes.query: The Ocean Biosphere 2 coral reef interior

scenes.text: In two thousand and seven the property was sold for fifty million dollars to a developer, with fifteen hundred homes and a resort hotel already approved for the land around it. Demolition was a real possibility.

The University of Arizona took over operations that same year. In twenty eleven they were given the building outright, along with twenty million dollars from Ed Bass to run it. He gave another thirty million in twenty seventeen.
It is open to the public today. About a hundred thousand people a year walk through it.

scenes.text: And inside, they built something called the Landscape Evolution Observatory. Three artificial hillslopes, each thirty metres long, each filled a metre deep with five hundred tons of crushed basalt. Sterile ground up volcanic rock. Dead.
More than eighteen hundred sensors in each one, watching what happens when you add water to bare rock and wait.
What happened is that nobody put anything alive on those slopes, and life showed up anyway.

Cyanobacteria colonised the sterile basalt. Photosynthesising, nitrogen fixing crusts, forming on ground up rock, exactly the way they did on the early Earth. Mosses now blanket those slopes seasonally.
The principal investigator's summary of the result was three words. Life finds a way.
In April twenty twenty six they were funded to take the next step, and build miniature versions of those hillslopes running Martian atmosphere and Martian soil chemistry.

And in February twenty twenty six, for the first time in more than thirty years, they put corals back into the Biosphere Two ocean. A hundred and eight living fragments, from the Florida Keys and the Gulf of Mexico.
Columbia used that same water, thirty years ago, to prove that carbon dioxide kills reefs. Today it is being used to find the ones that survive.
I want to tell you what I actually think, because I have spent a long time with this one.

scenes.text: Biosphere Two is remembered as a joke. There is a Pauly Shore movie about it, with a four percent score on Rotten Tomatoes and a one out of a hundred on Metacritic, which ties it for the worst reviewed film on that entire website. They shot it at a water reclamation plant in Van Nuys, because the real Biosphere Two turned them down.

Here is the thing about the joke. Biosphere Two failed at the thing it was sold as. It could not keep eight people fed and breathing for two years without help. That is true and there is no way around it.
scenes.videoQuery: Biosphere 2 space frame glazing lattice interior looking up

scenes.text: But a failure that teaches you something real is not a stunt. It is an experiment. And the discovery it produced, that a sealed world's oxygen can vanish into its own walls while its carbon dioxide reading stays flat and reassuring, is cited in the reference list of the very paper that condemned it.
Nobody would have predicted that. Nobody did predict it. And nobody could have found it in a building that was even slightly less well sealed.
scenes.videoQuery: sunlight through greenhouse glass panes reflection

scenes.text: Bad engineering. Worse governance. Genuine science. And a building that has outlived every single reason people had for laughing at it.
Jane Poynter said something about coming out that I cannot stop thinking about. For two years, she said, I'd been seeing people through the glass.

When visitors came, there was a window with a telephone on the outside and a telephone on the inside. And you would put your hand flat against the pane, and they would put theirs against it on the other side, and that was hello.
scenes.query: hand pressed against glass window pane
scenes.cap: They called it the biospherian handshake.

scenes.text: Eight people spent two years learning, in the most literal way anybody ever has, that air is not a given. That it is made, constantly, by things too small to see, and can be taken away by a wall that has not finished drying.

scenes.text: They built a second Earth to find out how the first one works. It didn't work. That is how they found out.
If the idea of microbes quietly rewriting an atmosphere got to you, there is a version of that story on a scale you will not believe, and it involves the Sun.
I made a video about whether the sun killing microbe in Project Hail Mary could actually exist. Real astrobiology, real extremophiles, and an answer that surprised me. It is on screen now.
And if you want more of these, the ones built out of the actual papers rather than the headlines, subscribe to mindwired. Thanks for watching.
